He also said he no longer suffers from the "jawthritis" that some cited as the culprit for his 2007 defeat, which snapped his six-year winning streak at Coney Island. Chestnut, for his part, said he had no intention of ceding the coveted mustard yellow belt -- competitive eating's answer to golf's green jacket. He is setting his sights this year on 68 hot dogs in 10 minutes. Saturday's competition will be partially about redemption for Chestnut, too. In May, he suffered a stinging defeat to Kobayashi in a loss he said "really set a fire underneath me" and "made me hungry for this contest." Chestnut revealed the extreme dietary regimen he is following in the days leading up to the contest. He said he is sticking to water to make sure he is "empty" when the mountain of hot dogs is placed in front of him. In addition to Chestnut, Kobayashi admitted to keeping a watchful eye on 32-year-old Tim "Eater X" Janus, whose signature painted face was described by Major League Eating impresario Richard Shea as an attempt to mask his "inner torment." In a recent trial round, Janus downed a personal-best 55 hot dogs -- a weiner's throw from the 59 that Chestnut and Kobayashi wolfed down last year. As a lead-in to the main event, Major League Eating on Friday will hold a first-of-its-kind "cross-species" eating contest between three competitive eaters and three Asian elephants. MLE's Shea described it as the realization of one of his two lifelong dreams, the other being a scenario in which a dozen competitive eaters eat the entire contents of a convenience store. Twenty finalists will compete in the championship on Saturday. They were culled from 18 preliminary contests and comprise a Who's Who of the world of competitive eating. For people who stuff their faces with record-breaking quantities of food, many of the contestants at the weigh-in boasted surprisingly svelte physiques. Juliet Lee, a 44-year-old Maryland salon owner fresh off the feat of downing 13.23 pounds of cranberry sauce in 8 minutes, clocked in at a mere 105 pounds. Kobayashi, at 123 pounds, lifted his T-shirt to reveal the sort of chiseled abdomen one would expect at a bodybuilding competition. Others contestants were not quite as disconcertingly trim. Fearsome world matzo ball-eating champion Eric "Badlands" Booker tips the scales at 400 pounds.

NEW YORK (CNN) — Joey Chestnut, the defending hot dog-eating champion, and his Japanese rival, Takeru Kobayashi, tried to intimidate one another Thursday during the weigh-in for the 94th Nathan’s Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog-Eating Contest. As part of an official faceoff, the two competitive eaters locked eyes in a prolonged, threatening stare.

In the previous year’s competition, Chestnut—then a 25-year-old civil engineering student at San Jose State University—narrowly defeated the 31-year-old Kobayashi in a tiebreaker after each had eaten 59 hot dogs. It marked Chestnut’s second close victory over Kobayashi in two consecutive years.

Kobayashi promised to settle the score on Saturday. He also said he had recovered from the so-called “jawthritis” that some blamed for his 2007 loss, which ended his six-year run as champion at Coney Island.

Chestnut, meanwhile, made clear that he did not plan to surrender the prized mustard-yellow championship belt, competitive eating’s equivalent of golf’s green jacket. His target this year is 68 hot dogs within 10 minutes.

The event also offers Chestnut a chance to redeem himself. Kobayashi handed him a painful defeat in May, a loss Chestnut said renewed his motivation and intensified his desire to win this contest.

Chestnut also disclosed the severe pre-contest diet he follows. In the days before the event, he consumes only water so that his stomach will be empty when the large serving of hot dogs appears before him.

Kobayashi said Chestnut is not the only competitor he is monitoring closely. He is also watching 32-year-old Tim “Eater X” Janus. Richard Shea, the impresario behind Major League Eating, said Janus’ trademark painted face is meant to conceal the competitor’s emotional anguish.

During a recent practice attempt, Janus consumed a personal record of 55 hot dogs, putting him only four short of the 59 eaten by both Chestnut and Kobayashi the year before.

Before the main competition, Major League Eating will stage its first “cross-species” eating event on Friday, featuring three professional eaters and three Asian elephants. Shea called the spectacle the fulfillment of one of his two lifelong ambitions. His other dream is to have 12 competitive eaters consume everything inside a convenience store.

Saturday’s championship will include 20 finalists selected through 18 qualifying events. Together, they represent many of the most prominent names in competitive eating.

Despite regularly consuming record-setting amounts of food, several contestants at the weigh-in had unexpectedly lean builds. Juliet Lee, a 44-year-old salon owner from Maryland, weighed just 105 pounds, even though she had recently eaten 13.23 pounds of cranberry sauce in eight minutes.

Kobayashi weighed 123 pounds and raised his shirt to display sharply defined abdominal muscles more typical of a bodybuilding contest.

Not every entrant was similarly slim, however. Eric “Badlands” Booker, the formidable world matzo ball-eating champion, weighed 400 pounds.

The two champions posed for cameras ahead of Saturday’s 10-minute contest at Coney Island, where thousands of spectators are expected to watch competitors consume as many hot dogs and buns as possible.

Chestnut enters as the two-time defending champion. The American ended Kobayashi’s six-year winning streak in 2007, then defeated the Japanese star again in dramatic fashion a year later. In 2008, the rivals finished regulation tied at 59 hot dogs before Chestnut won a five-dog eat-off.

Despite the ceremonial weigh-in, body size has rarely predicted success in the event. Chestnut is the larger of the two men, while Kobayashi built his reputation by combining speed, flexibility and an eating technique that helped transform the contest into an international spectacle.

Kobayashi dominated Nathan’s from 2001 through 2006 and remains one of the sport’s most recognizable figures. Chestnut, meanwhile, has become the face of a new generation of American competitive eaters and will compete with a supportive Coney Island crowd behind him.

Both men expressed confidence during the pre-contest festivities, though neither revealed much about strategy. Competitors typically spend months training their stomachs and refining methods for swallowing quickly, including separating the hot dogs from their buns and dipping the bread in water.

The rivalry has brought heightened attention to a contest that began as a holiday attraction and has grown into a nationally televised Fourth of July tradition.

For Chestnut, Saturday offers a chance to secure a third consecutive Mustard Belt. For Kobayashi, it is an opportunity to reclaim the title he once seemed certain to hold indefinitely.

After two straight years of close competition, organizers and fans are expecting another tense showdown — one likely to be decided one bite at a time.

counterfactuals.output:
## Chestnut Devours Record 68 Hot Dogs to Retain Nathan’s Crown

**CONEY ISLAND, N.Y., July 4, 2009** — Joey Chestnut once again outlasted Takeru Kobayashi in competitive eating’s premier rivalry Saturday, consuming a world-record **68 hot dogs and buns in 10 minutes** to win his third consecutive Nathan’s Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog-Eating Contest.

Chestnut’s total surpassed the 66-dog record he had established under the contest’s former 12-minute format in 2007. More importantly, it gave the defending champion a clear victory over Kobayashi, the six-time Nathan’s winner whose **64½ hot dogs and buns** would have been enough to dominate almost any other field.

The result reinforced the sport’s new order. Kobayashi, once considered nearly unbeatable at Coney Island, had ruled the event from 2001 through 2006. Chestnut ended that streak in 2007, then defeated the Japanese star again in dramatic fashion in 2008, when the two finished regulation tied at 59 and Chestnut won a five-hot-dog overtime eat-off.

This time, no tiebreaker was needed.

Chestnut and Kobayashi quickly separated themselves from the rest of the competitors, matching a punishing pace through the early stages. Using his familiar technique of eating the hot dogs separately from the buns and dipping the bread in liquid to make it easier to swallow, Chestnut maintained enough speed late in the contest to create a decisive margin.

When the 10-minute clock expired, officials credited the Californian with 68, putting him 3½ ahead of Kobayashi. Chestnut raised the Mustard Belt before a packed Independence Day crowd near Nathan’s original Coney Island restaurant.

“Sixty-eight” immediately became the new benchmark for the event and a striking demonstration of how far the Chestnut-Kobayashi rivalry had pushed competitive eating. Kobayashi’s runner-up total was itself extraordinary, but for a third straight year it was not enough.

### Kobayashi remains a formidable challenger

Although the defeat extended Kobayashi’s Nathan’s losing streak, his performance showed that he remained Chestnut’s most serious threat.

Kobayashi revolutionized the contest at the start of the decade. In 2001, he consumed 50 hot dogs and buns, nearly doubling the previous record and introducing a more athletic, highly technical style to an event that had previously been treated largely as a holiday spectacle. He went on to win six consecutive Mustard Belts and became the sport’s first international superstar.

By 2009, however, Chestnut had met and surpassed that standard. Bigger and increasingly efficient, he proved capable not only of matching Kobayashi’s early pace but also of sustaining it through the decisive final minutes.

The 2009 contest therefore represented more than another narrow loss for Kobayashi. It confirmed that Chestnut’s victories in the previous two years were not isolated upsets. The American had become the man to beat.

### “Eater X” brings an outsider’s threat

Away from the two favorites, **Tim “Eater X” Janus** entered as one of the field’s most intriguing dark horses. Janus, known for competing with his face painted in a distinctive red, black and white design, was already an accomplished Major League Eating veteran with victories and high finishes across a variety of foods.

His versatility made him a plausible challenger if either Chestnut or Kobayashi faltered. Janus possessed the capacity, speed and experience to remain near the front of an elite field, and his theatrical persona made him one of the contest’s most recognizable figures.

But the leaders left little room for an upset. Janus produced another strong performance and remained among the event’s top-tier eaters, yet he could not match the record-breaking tempo established by Chestnut and Kobayashi. As in much of competitive eating during this period, the battle behind the two superstars became a contest of its own.

Janus’s showing nevertheless reinforced his standing as more than a novelty act. “Eater X” combined showmanship with genuine competitive ability, and he remained the sort of entrant capable of capitalizing if the favorites stumbled.

### A rivalry at full boil

Nathan’s annual July Fourth contest, staged at the corner of Surf and Stillwell avenues, had by 2009 become a nationally televised sports spectacle. Thousands crowded the Coney Island intersection while a much larger audience watched on ESPN.

The central attraction was the contrast between its two leading men: Chestnut, the powerful American defending champion, and Kobayashi, the lighter, technically precise former ruler trying to reclaim his title. Janus and the rest of the field added depth and uncertainty, but the championship again came down to the era’s defining rivalry.

Chestnut’s 68-hot-dog performance provided the emphatic conclusion. After a one-dog victory in 2007 and an overtime escape in 2008, he finally created clear separation from Kobayashi while setting a record under the shortened 10-minute format.

For Chestnut, the afternoon delivered a third straight Mustard Belt and a new world record. For Kobayashi, it was another remarkable performance overshadowed by his rival. And for Janus, it was proof that even an elite dark horse faced an immense challenge in breaking through while the two giants of the sport were operating near their peaks.

## Heavy Eaters, Lightweights at Nathan’s Weigh-In

The scales came out, the cameras crowded in and the world’s top competitive eaters once again proved that appearances can be wonderfully misleading.

At the official weigh-in for Nathan’s Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog Eating Contest, the contenders looked less like walking refrigerators than a collection of cyclists, accountants and people who might politely decline dessert. Yet these deceptively ordinary physiques belong to athletes capable of consuming a backyard barbecue’s entire inventory in 10 minutes.

Defending champion Joey Chestnut arrived with a suitably outrageous target: 68 hot dogs and buns. It is the sort of number that sounds less like lunch than a clerical error, but Chestnut spoke of it as a realistic goal. Having turned speed-eating into a blend of conditioning, technique and gastrointestinal brinkmanship, he seemed ready to push the mustard-yellow belt—and the human digestive system—into new territory.

His great rival, Takeru Kobayashi, supplied the weigh-in’s comeback story. The Japanese star said he had recovered from the jaw ailment nicknamed “jawthritis,” a condition that had threatened the most important piece of equipment in his profession. For a competitive eater, jaw trouble is roughly equivalent to a concert pianist spraining all 10 fingers. Now healthy again, Kobayashi appeared prepared to chew, dunk and swallow his way back to the top.

The spectacle will not end with humans competing against humans. Organizers also discussed a planned humans-versus-elephants eating event, an idea that sounds as though it was developed after someone asked, “How can we make competitive eating seem even more unreasonable?” The obvious advantage belongs to the elephants, although the humans will presumably counter with strategy, speed and an alarming willingness to train for this sort of thing.

Perhaps the strangest sight at the weigh-in was how unstrange the eaters looked. Many were trim, even athletic. Competitive eating’s elite have long confounded the assumption that champions must be enormous. Their secret is not sheer body mass but stomach capacity, rhythm, breathing, hand speed and the ability to remain calm while doing something every instinct says should stop several dozen hot dogs earlier.

That contrast is part of Nathan’s enduring carnival appeal: modest-looking competitors, absurd quantities of food and stakes treated with Olympic seriousness. When the countdown begins at Coney Island, Chestnut will chase 68, Kobayashi will test his repaired jaw, and the rest of the field will try to turn lunch into legend.

The scales may tell us what these competitors weigh. They offer absolutely no clue how much they can eat.

### Tension rises before Nathan’s July 4 hot-dog contest

NEW YORK — The psychological contest began before anyone touched a hot dog.

At the official weigh-in and staredown for the 2024 Nathan’s Famous Fourth of July International Hot Dog Eating Contest, leading competitors stood nose-to-nose, attempting to project confidence before the 10-minute spectacle at Coney Island.

Major League Eating chairman Richard Shea described the ritual as an important piece of competitive theater: the fixed gaze, posturing and refusal to flinch establish the mental pecking order before contestants reach the table.

The men’s competition was unusually open because Joey Chestnut, winner of 16 Nathan’s titles, was excluded after agreeing to promote a rival plant-based hot-dog brand. Chestnut won in 2023 with 62 hot dogs and buns and holds the event record of 76, set in 2021.

Shea likened Chestnut’s absence to a great musician missing from the stage, while arguing that it had given the rest of the field a rare sense of possibility.

Among the principal men’s contenders were:

- **Geoffrey Esper**, a methodical Massachusetts eater long ranked among Chestnut’s closest challengers.
- **James Webb**, an Australian known for his speed and a growing collection of eating records.
- **Patrick Bertoletti**, a veteran Chicago competitor returning to Nathan’s after years away.
- **Nick Wehry**, another highly ranked American with repeated top finishes at Coney Island.

The women’s side offered a more clearly defined rivalry. **Miki Sudo**, a nine-time champion and holder of the women’s record of 48½ hot dogs and buns, again faced Japan’s **Mayoi Ebihara**, whose animated style and rapid improvement had made her Sudo’s most dangerous challenger.

Shea portrayed that matchup as genuinely chilly rather than manufactured promotion, saying there was “no love lost” between the two. He characterized Sudo as controlled and technically polished, while Ebihara brought unpredictability and visible intensity.

The staredown itself lasted only moments, but Shea treated it as the opening exchange in what Major League Eating routinely presents as equal parts sport, endurance ordeal and carnival drama. The real decision would come July 4 on the corner of Surf and Stillwell avenues, where competitors would have 10 minutes to consume as many hot dogs and buns as possible.
